client: I've been feeling completely overwhelmed since I started this new job at the tech startup. No matter how many hours I put in, I keep falling behind on my project deadlines, and it's making me question whether I'm even cut out for this role. To be honest, I'm not sure talking about it will help - the deadlines aren't going to change, and I just need to work harder.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a heavy weight of self-doubt and pressure, and your tone suggests this is really taking an emotional toll on you. While it's understandable to feel overwhelmed in a new role, I wonder if there might be more balanced ways to view this situation - perhaps you're holding yourself to unrealistic standards or overlooking the challenges that come with adjusting to any new position.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I get what you're saying about unrealistic standards, but I don't think that's the issue here. Everyone else at the company seems to be handling their workload just fine, and I'm the only one struggling to keep up. It's not just about adjusting - I genuinely feel like I'm not smart enough or skilled enough for this job, and it's making me dread going to work every day.
therapist: Your voice carries a deep sense of discouragement and self-doubt, and it's clear this situation is weighing heavily on you. When we compare ourselves to others, it's easy to overlook that every person's journey is unique - what you're interpreting as personal inadequacy might actually be the natural challenges of finding your footing in a new environment. Let's explore what evidence you have that supports or challenges this belief about not being skilled enough.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: Evidence? Well, I keep missing deadlines and my manager has had to talk to me twice about my productivity. That seems like pretty clear evidence to me. I know you're saying not to compare myself to others, but it's hard not to when I see my teammates completing their tasks on time while I'm constantly falling behind. It feels like I'm the weak link in the team.
therapist: I hear the frustration and defeat in your voice as you describe these challenges, and it's understandable you'd feel this way given the feedback you've received. While the productivity conversations are certainly important to address, I wonder if we might look at this situation differently - could there be other factors at play, like unclear expectations, insufficient onboarding, or simply needing more time to adjust to this particular work environment?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess the onboarding was pretty rushed - I got two days of training before being thrown into projects. But shouldn't I have been able to pick things up faster? The other new hires who started around the same time seem to be doing fine. Maybe I'm just not as quick a learner as I thought I was.
therapist: I can hear the tension and self-criticism in your voice as you share this - it seems you're really putting a lot of pressure on yourself to perform at the same level as others right away. Given how rushed the onboarding was, perhaps we could reframe this not as a personal failing, but as a mismatch between the training provided and what you needed to succeed. Everyone learns at different paces, and comparing your progress to others might not be giving you credit for the challenges you've faced.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I see what you're saying about it being a mismatch, but I'm still worried it reflects poorly on me. Even if the onboarding was rushed, shouldn't I have been able to figure things out on my own? I feel like I'm making excuses when I blame the training. At the end of the day, I'm still the one not meeting expectations.
therapist: Your voice sounds quite distressed as you say this, and I can hear how deeply this is affecting your self-confidence. While you're worried about making excuses, I notice you're also holding yourself to an exceptionally high standard - expecting yourself to compensate for inadequate training while still maintaining the same performance as others who may have had different support systems or prior experience.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I never really thought about it that way... but I guess you're right that I am being hard on myself. It's just that in my last job, I was always the top performer, so struggling like this is new and scary for me. The thought of asking for more help makes me feel weak though - like I should be able to handle this on my own.
therapist: Your voice speeds up as you talk about asking for help, and I can hear how uncomfortable this idea makes you feel. It makes perfect sense that this would be scary after being used to excelling - that transition from top performer to needing support can be really unsettling. Might it be possible that asking for help isn't a sign of weakness, but rather a smart strategy to get you back to performing at your best?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I know logically that asking for help makes sense, but every time I go to do it, I freeze up. What if my manager just thinks I'm incompetent? I keep imagining them saying "We hired you to solve problems, not create more work for others." Maybe I should just push through on my own until I figure it out.
therapist: I can hear the anxiety in your quickened speech and higher pitch as you share these worries - it's clear this fear of being seen as incompetent is really holding you back. While your mind is presenting you with worst-case scenarios, perhaps we could explore whether there's any evidence that your manager would actually respond that way, or if this might be more about the pressure you're putting on yourself.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Honestly, my manager has actually been pretty reasonable in our past conversations, even when giving feedback. But I still can't shake this fear that this will be the time they lose patience with me. It's like no matter how understanding they've been before, I'm convinced the next conversation will be the one where they finally realize they made a mistake hiring me.
therapist: Your voice sounds tense and rushed as you share this, and I can hear how much this fear is consuming you, even when your logical mind knows your manager has been reasonable before. This anticipation of rejection seems to be creating a lot of distress - let's explore together why you might be holding onto this belief so strongly, even when the evidence suggests otherwise.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech

client: I guess part of me feels like I've been getting by on luck so far, and that eventually people will see through the facade. Even though my manager has been understanding, I keep waiting for the other shoe to drop. It's like I can't trust that I actually belong here, even though I worked hard to get this job.
therapist: Your voice sounds urgent and strained as you share this, and I can hear how painful this feeling of being an imposter really is for you. It's striking how even your past successes can't quiet that inner voice telling you you don't truly belong - I wonder if we might explore where this deep-seated distrust in your own abilities comes from?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client: I never really thought about where it comes from... but now that you mention it, I grew up with parents who were never satisfied no matter how well I did in school. There was always "room for improvement." Maybe that's why I can't accept my own successes now. But isn't that just making excuses? Other people had tough childhoods too and they don't struggle like this.
therapist: Your voice sounds both rushed and distressed as you make this connection, and I can hear how painful this realization is for you - it seems these early experiences of never feeling "good enough" continue to affect you deeply today. While it's understandable you'd compare yourself to others who had difficult childhoods, everyone's journey with self-worth is unique, and recognizing these patterns isn't making excuses - it's showing self-awareness that could help you break free from this cycle of self-doubt.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech
